newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: SOCCER-DUKLA MOVE TO 1ST DIVISION, CAN A NEW RECORD BE FAR OFF.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DUKLA MOVE TO 1ST DIVISION, CAN A NEW RECORD BE FAR OFF.

text.p: Dukla Prague, once the pride of Czech soccer that fell from grace -- and the first division -- in 1994, has been promoted back to the country's highest league for the 1997-98 season.

The team, which inspired a cult following abroad which shaped the quirky Half Man-Half Biscuit record "All I want for Christmas is a Dukla Prague away kit" in the 1980s, fell on hard times after the fall of Communism in 1989.

Free-market realities replaced Soviet-style sports funding and the army team, named after a mountain pass in former federation partner Slovakia where the Czechs and Slovaks battled Nazis to the death, went into a freefall that saw it eventually land in the lowly third division.
But all that changed when local entrepreneur Bohumil Duricko recently took over the team.

"We did all we could to save Dukla football but we had little time," said former Dukla director Vaclav Samek. "Mr. Duricko's money saved Dukla. For that we will thank him until the rest of our lives."

Late on Tuesday, Dukla's re-entry into first division life became official when the league played its final round. Dukla ran away with the second league title, which it officially claimed on Sunday. It will also contest the final of the Czech-Moravian Cup against Slavia Prague on Sunday.

European Cup semifinalists in 1967, Dukla Prague won the Czechoslovak first division championship 11 times and finished runners-up seven times after the club was established by the Ministry of Defence in 1948.

At their peak, life was easy for Dukla. With the likes of Josef Masopust, European Footballer of the Year in 1962, and Zdenek Nehoda, a record 90 caps for his country, they would fill the major 25,000-seat venues.
And when they needed new players they could ignore the transfer market by simply drafting them into the army where they became the country's best-compensated athletes.
All of that came crashing down when other teams, such as Sparta Prague and Slavia, picked up major sponsors while few would touch Dukla, tainted by its overtly communist past.
By the end of the 1993-4 season, when they slipped to the third division and were forced to sell off players, the spectators were almost outnumbered by the stadium staff.
But along came Duricko, a knight in shining armour whose energy, and more importantly pocketbook, restored the lustre to a tarnished team.
Duricko's first move to restore the club to former glories was to buy second division club FC Pribram. He merged the teams and then expropriated Pribram's spot in the higher league.

"Dukla has sent more players to the national team than any other and had more international success," he said. "We want to return the club to those traditions. To return to the first division would help create a new tradition."
It may take time to change the image at home, but ultimately, it may even lead to a return to the top flight of European soccer and, who knows, another cult record.
